Product E is a formulation specifically excluded from federal CSA scheduling under its applicable federal exemption record and is classified as Massachusetts Schedule VI. Product C is federally AND Massachusetts Schedule IV. Each prescription was issued March 1, 2026, contains any legally required information, has one refill remaining under the prescriber's directions, and is requested November 18, 2026. No separate continuity, emergency or new-prescription authority applies. Which decisions are supported? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1308.31–1308.32 (exempted prescription products; formulation-dependent); 21 CFR 1306.22(a); 247 CMR 9.04(12)–(13); M.G.L. c.94C §23
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 9.04(12), 21 CFR 1306.22(a), 1308.31-.32; product-specific federal exemption assumed as given
questions.scope_or_source_caveat: Fictional product E is not verified against real exemption-list formulations/NDCs; conclusions apply only to the explicitly assumed classifications.

options.option_text: An extra authorized refill always overrides both products' expiration or issuance-validity limits because it is part of the original prescription.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A prescriber's refill count is necessary but does not defeat statutory prescription validity limits.
options.independent_option_analysis: Authorized refill count cannot override legal expiration.

options.option_text: Product E may still be considered for its remaining authorized Schedule VI refill under the Massachusetts one-year validity rule, if no other restriction applies.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The case expressly establishes federally exempt status for this formulation and MA Schedule VI classification; state Schedule VI validity and refill authority apply to its dispensing decision.
options.independent_option_analysis: MA Schedule VI default one-year validity if the question's fictional exempt-product classification is assumed.

options.option_text: Product C must be handled under Schedule IV validity/refill limits; the eight-month-old original prescription cannot supply a new refill.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Federal 21 CFR 1306.22(a) closes Schedule III/IV prescriptions six months after issuance; remaining written refills do not extend the clock.
options.independent_option_analysis: Federally Schedule IV cannot be refilled eight months after issue.

options.option_text: Any product ever containing a formerly scheduled ingredient is automatically subject to its ingredient's Schedule IV federal refill limit even when this exact combination is exempt.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Federal exemption status is product/formulation-specific; the table explicitly states the supplied legally effective classification.
options.independent_option_analysis: A federally exempt formulation is not automatically controlled solely by a scheduled ingredient.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy compounds a patient-specific NONPRESERVED aqueous oral suspension. The formula meets the USP <795> default requirements for this dosage form, which would ordinarily allow up to a 14-day refrigerated BUD in the absence of better data. However, specific trustworthy stability data for THIS formulation establish that potency falls below specification after FIVE refrigerated days. What BUD should the pharmacist consider?
questions.author_citation: USP <795> §10/Table 4 (official Nov. 2023, shorter stability governs); 247 CMR 9.01(3)

options.option_text: Fourteen days because the chapter's default BUD is a guaranteed minimum regardless of demonstrated instability.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A default table maximum never overrides an earlier demonstrated stability failure for that actual formulation.

options.option_text: Thirty-five days because this preparation is aqueous and all aqueous liquids have the preserved-formulation category BUD.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The 35-day default applies to properly preserved aqueous dosage forms, not this nonpreserved suspension.

options.option_text: Use the supplier's longest unexpired ingredient date, even if the finished mixture fails stability earlier.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Ingredient shelf life is not proof of final compounded-formulation stability.

options.option_text: No more than five refrigerated days, subject to all other applicable limits, rather than the longer default period.
options.original_rationale: Correct. USP <795> Table 4 says a shorter BUD is required where the actual formulation's chemical or physical stability is shorter.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts nonsterile-compounding pharmacy uses an established master formulation record for a 100-mL oral suspension. A new patient-specific preparation follows the same formula, but uses different ingredient LOTS and is prepared by a different qualified compounder. Under the Board's inspection expectations and applicable USP <795> record framework, which records are appropriate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.01(3); MA Board Retail Pharmacy Inspection Template items 92–93; USP <795> §§8–9, master formulation and compounding records
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 9.01(3), inspection items 92-93, Board Policy 2023-07 Section VI; MFR and each-preparation CR
questions.scope_or_source_caveat: Direct MA Board inspection/policy text supports tested rule; full subscription USP <795> text not authenticated.

options.option_text: Use only the master formulation record for all subsequent batches, because batch-specific details are already established by the first successful preparation.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The Board's retail inspection template requires a compounding record for every nonsterile preparation; an MFR is not a substitute for recording later lots and personnel.
options.independent_option_analysis: Master formula does not replace the preparation-specific compounding record.

options.option_text: Follow the established master formulation record and prepare a separate compounding record identifying the ingredients and lot information actually used for this preparation.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The reusable MFR describes the formulation and method; the preparation-specific CR captures this batch's ingredients, lot numbers and execution details.
options.independent_option_analysis: MFR reused; separate CR documents used lots and personnel.

options.option_text: Create a completely new master formulation solely because the same approved formula is made for a different patient's prescription.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A change of patient does not by itself require inventing a different formulation when the existing MFR remains applicable.
options.independent_option_analysis: New patient alone does not require a different formula/MFR.

options.option_text: Document the actual preparation date, compounder, measurements and finished preparation details in a compounding record linked to the correct formulation.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Massachusetts inspection standards require an MFR to be followed and a CR for each preparation, making the record traceable to the particular operation.
options.independent_option_analysis: CR must record preparation date, actual ingredients, compounder and traceability.

questions.question_stem: Before compounding an oral suspension, the compounder discovers that the balance failed its accuracy check and that yesterday's ingredient weights cannot be reconciled. The finished suspension looks normal. What should happen next?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.01(3); MA Board Retail Pharmacy Inspection Template (nonsterile compounding controls and records); applicable USP <795>
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 9.01(3); inspection item 87 equipment properly maintained and used; compounding quality/records
questions.scope_or_source_caveat: MA Board equipment/records expectations support the decision, but precise current USP <795> normative wording not directly available.

options.option_text: Release the preparation because a visual inspection substitutes for quantitative controls.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Appearance alone cannot establish accurate ingredient amounts when weighing equipment is unreliable.
options.independent_option_analysis: Visual appearance cannot establish accurate preparation after failed measuring equipment.

options.option_text: Hold the preparation and correct the weighing problem before release.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Reliable measuring equipment and traceable execution are essential to compliant nonsterile compounding.
options.independent_option_analysis: Correct action is hold and investigate/restore reliable measuring control.

options.option_text: Shorten the BUD and release the batch.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A shorter BUD does not establish accurate ingredient weights after a failed measuring-equipment check.
options.independent_option_analysis: Shortening BUD does not correct erroneous unknown ingredient mass.

options.option_text: Delete the incorrect measurements from the record and retain only the final appearance.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Removing data undermines traceability and does not resolve the failed balance check.
options.independent_option_analysis: Erasing measurements is incompatible with traceable compounding records.

questions.question_stem: At a Massachusetts Category 2 sterile-compounding pharmacy, a technician passes a media-fill simulation but the gloved fingertip/thumb sampling collected immediately afterward exceeds the applicable action level. The supervisor suggests closing the assessment as a pass because the media-fill container showed no growth. Under the official USP <797> interpretation, what is the BEST response?
questions.author_citation: USP <797> §§2.2–2.3 and 20; USP official FAQ (Dec 11, 2023), Q53; WA DOH 2026 USP <797> self-inspection addendum, §2.3 quoted text

options.option_text: Close the assessment as passed because the media-fill culture is a more direct sterility test than the glove sample.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Passing the media fill does not cancel a separate failed post-media-fill gloved-fingertip/thumb component.

options.option_text: Repeat only the media fill next week and disregard the glove finding once the new simulated preparation shows no growth.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Repeating an unrelated passing component does not resolve the failed gloved-fingertip sampling or required investigation.

options.option_text: Assume USP mandates automatic shutdown of all compounding across the facility until every worker completes three entirely new media fills.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. USP FAQ Q53 states that the chapter does not itself impose universal automatic cessation; the facility must evaluate the failure, take and document appropriate corrective action.

options.option_text: Record an overall competency failure, investigate the cause, and document corrective actions and appropriate reassessment.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The post-media-fill fingertip component is independently required; a failure makes the aseptic manipulation competency fail, and corrective-action investigation and records are required.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts Category 2 sterile compounding pharmacy uses a commercially manufactured SINGLE-DOSE vial as a component for future CSPs. At 8:00 a.m. a qualified compounder first punctures its intact septum inside a certified ISO Class 5 PEC. The vial is then stored OUTSIDE the ISO Class 5 PEC, at the manufacturer's specified refrigerated temperature; the closure remains intact and all other component requirements are satisfied. At 4:00 p.m. the same day the pharmacy plans another compounding use. Which conclusions are supported by USP's official <797> FAQ? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: Initial puncture in ISO Class 5 with suitable storage can support using the vial for up to 12 hours after first entry, assuming no shorter stability or other restriction applies.
options.original_rationale: Correct. FAQ Q186 establishes the initial-entry condition and up-to-12-hour component-use period, subject to maintained storage conditions.

options.option_text: Once the vial leaves the PEC after puncture, it must be discarded immediately because all post-entry storage is required to remain in ISO Class 5 air.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. FAQ Q186 says opened or punctured conventional single-dose containers may be stored outside the PEC under conditions.

options.option_text: The pharmacy's 4:00 p.m. use may remain within the in-use period; the container must still be properly handled in the PEC when entered for compounding.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Eight hours have passed since first entry, less than the conditional 12-hour maximum.

options.option_text: An opened single-dose glass ampule may be saved for twelve hours by refrigerating the open neck, because ampules follow the same resealable-vial rule.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. FAQ Q186 distinguishes opened ampules: they cannot be stored after opening.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts sterile-compounding pharmacy plans to make a Category 2 injectable preparation. The active ingredient is a NONSTERILE bulk powder, but the diluent and receiving IV bag are sterile. The technician proposes mixing in an ISO Class 5 hood and then treating the preparation as though it was compounded only from sterile ingredients, without any sterilization step. What is the best response?
questions.author_citation: USP <797> §§10.2, 11, 14 (official Nov. 1, 2023) and USP official FAQ on sterilization; 247 CMR 9.01(3)

options.option_text: Accept the plan because mixing a nonsterile powder inside ISO Class 5 air instantly converts it to a sterile starting ingredient.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Cleanroom air is not a sterilization method, and the starting powder remains a nonsterile component.

options.option_text: Require a suitable validated sterilization process and release controls for the CSP made with nonsterile starting powder.
options.original_rationale: Correct. USP <797> recognizes nonsterile starting components but requires an appropriate sterilization process and assessment of endotoxin and other risks.

options.option_text: Select the longest Category 2 BUD because one sterile ingredient and one sterile bag outweigh the nonsterile powder.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The presence of any nonsterile starting component affects controls, sterilization requirements and BUD eligibility.

options.option_text: Label the final bag sterile solely because the pharmacist signs the compounding record, even without validating processing.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A sign-off does not replace the sterile process and required release checks.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts sterile compounding pharmacy formerly produced Category 2 NONHAZARDOUS CSPs under a validated ISO Class 5 primary engineering control (PEC) inside a properly classified cleanroom suite. After renovation, the same PEC is moved into an UNCLASSIFIED segregated compounding area (SCA) while all personnel qualifications remain current. Management proposes assigning the same Category 2 refrigerated BUDs as before solely because the hood still meets ISO Class 5. What is the best response?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: USP <797> FAQ and MA Board Sterile Compounding Inspection Tool class 2 vs SCA; directly subscribed chapter not authenticated
questions.scope_or_source_caveat: HOLD exact normative USP <797> paragraphs/standard before full legal clearance.

options.option_text: Keep the old BUDs, since the ISO Class 5 primary airflow is the only relevant classification for every CSP category.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The surrounding environmental classification and location requirements matter; ISO 5 PEC status alone does not preserve every Category 2 environmental condition.
options.independent_option_analysis: ISO5 PEC alone does not create classified cleanroom setting.

options.option_text: Apply the old BUDs if staff have passed their competency evaluations, because trained staff replace the need for a classified buffer room.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Personnel competency is required but does not substitute for the facility's engineering and environmental standards.
options.independent_option_analysis: Personnel competence does not replace appropriate room classification.

options.option_text: Requalify the changed facility and reassess category and BUD; an ISO 5 PEC in an SCA does not retain Category 2 BUDs automatically.
options.original_rationale: Correct. An ISO 5 PEC in an SCA is not the same environment as a classified cleanroom suite for default Category 2 limits; changes require qualification and reassessment.
options.independent_option_analysis: Requalification / category and BUD reassessment supported, but exact full USP normative clauses not directly confirmed.

options.option_text: Use the maximal Category 2 BUD whenever preparations contain only sterile manufactured ingredients, regardless of room classification.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Sterile starting components and a certified PEC do not independently grant Category 2 BUD authority absent the required setting and controls.
options.independent_option_analysis: Sterile ingredients alone do not confer extended Category2 BUD in unclassified SCA.

questions.question_stem: A community pharmacy has classified a medication it stocks as a hazardous drug using its current hazardous-drug list. It ordinarily dispenses intact manufacturer-finished tablets under an assessment-of-risk program. An individual prescription now requires the tablets to be CRUSHED and mixed into a patient-specific oral suspension; staff propose using the same ordinary counter used for intact tablets and skipping additional containment because the drug has not changed. According to the Massachusetts Board's USP <800> advisory, which steps are appropriate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.01(3); MA Board Advisory USP <800> in Community Pharmacies (revised Feb. 3, 2022), pp.1-3; USP <800>

options.option_text: Treat crushing as equivalent to dispensing an intact tablet with no additional exposure assessment.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Crushing changes exposure risks and triggers the Board advisory's hazardous-compounding discussion.

options.option_text: Evaluate the hazardous-drug risk and apply the required containment controls for the crushing and compounding process.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The advisory identifies HD crushing or capsule opening for compounded preparations as a containment-requiring situation.

options.option_text: Conclude that USP <800> does not apply to community pharmacies as long as they do not prepare sterile products.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The Board explicitly applies HD handling expectations to community pharmacies including nonsterile compounding.

options.option_text: Ensure the designated responsible person and applicable work-practice, facility, and staff controls are in place.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The Board advisory requires a formal HD program and designated trained responsible person.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts sterile-compounding pharmacy prepares hazardous drugs in a suitable containment PEC. The staff propose a cleaning procedure that applies 70% isopropyl alcohol as the ONLY step because it disinfects work surfaces. Which statements reflect the distinct hazardous-drug controls described by USP <800> and OSHA's guidance? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: USP <800> §15 and Table 5 (official USP 2019 revision bulletin; 2026 text version not authenticated); OSHA Hazardous Drugs: Controlling Occupational Exposure; USP January 2026 <800> FAQ status

options.option_text: Using alcohol to disinfect alone is proven to deactivate all currently listed hazardous drugs.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. OSHA notes that alcohol-based disinfection does not automatically deactivate hazardous residues and may spread contamination.

options.option_text: A visibly clean work surface may skip hazardous-drug decontamination because microbial disinfection is the only contamination concern.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Visible appearance does not prove absence of hazardous drug residue or eliminate exposure controls.

options.option_text: Deactivation, decontamination, and cleaning address hazardous-drug residues and soil, while subsequent disinfection in sterile compounding addresses microbial contamination.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The distinct processes cannot be assumed equivalent; OSHA describes deactivation/decontamination/cleaning followed by disinfection for sterile work areas.

options.option_text: The facility should assess its drug, materials and manufacturer instructions to choose appropriate residue-control steps rather than relying on one disinfectant alone.
options.original_rationale: Correct. No single method has been found to deactivate all hazardous drugs; controls must fit actual substances and equipment.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts sterile-compounding facility receives a FINAL above-action-level VIABLE environmental monitoring result for its ISO Class 7 BUFFER ROOM. A separate nonviable particle counter has not detected any excursion in the nearby ISO Class 8 room. The facility considers compounding during corrective action; no Board-specific instruction allowing longer BUDs has been issued. Which responses align with Board Policy 2026-03? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: MA Board Policy 2026-03 §§III–VI (action-level environmental monitoring, adopted Sept. 3, 2026)

options.option_text: Continue ordinary long Category 2 BUDs because only the nonviable particles were within limits.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The viable excursion triggers specific remedial limits, regardless of separate particle results.

options.option_text: Assess the viable excursion, implement remediation/CAPA, and arrange the required repeat environmental monitoring even if the separate nonviable count is normal.
options.original_rationale: Correct. A normal nonviable result does not nullify the independent viable action level; policy §§III–IV require assessment, remediation and resampling.

options.option_text: Declare the affected room fully cleared immediately because the ISO 8 area tested normally; resampling of the ISO 7 area is unnecessary.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Affected-area repeat environmental monitoring and CAPA cannot be waived by an unrelated room's result.

options.option_text: If the pharmacy resumes compounding during ISO 7 buffer-room remediation under policy conditions, limit applicable CSP BUDs to 24 hours room temperature or four days refrigerated.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Board Policy 2026-03 §V expressly caps buffer-room BUDs during remediation, absent contrary Board direction.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy conducts its controlled-substance stock reconciliation and finds 10 Schedule II tablets missing. The pharmacist immediately confirms that EIGHT tablets were actually dispensed under a documented prescription but posted to the wrong inventory record. The remaining TWO tablets cannot yet be accounted for, and there is no confirmed theft, diversion or significant loss determination. Under MA Board Policy 2026-01, what is the BEST next action regarding the Board loss report?
questions.author_citation: MA Board Policy 2026-01 §§II–III (adopted Mar. 26, 2026); 21 CFR 1301.76(b) (distinct federal reporting rule)

options.option_text: File a Board confirmed-theft report for all ten tablets immediately, because any first discrepancy automatically establishes employee diversion.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Initial discrepancy alone does not establish theft or confirmed loss; eight units have already been traced to a posting error.

options.option_text: Treat the discrepancy as fully resolved because finding one record error proves every missing unit has the same cause.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Two tablets remain unexplained and require further inventory reconciliation and assessment; unrelated errors cannot be assumed to explain them.

options.option_text: Ignore the two tablets until the next annual inventory because a quantity below three tablets is never significant.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The policy does not set a blanket 'three tablet' exemption; unexplained discrepancies require investigation and significance assessment.

options.option_text: Investigate and record the remaining two tablets, and determine whether a reportable loss is confirmed under applicable rules.
options.original_rationale: Correct. MA Board Policy 2026-01 states not to submit unconfirmed loss reports, but still requires action for confirmed theft/diversion or significant losses; DEA and other agencies have distinct rules.

questions.question_stem: The pharmacy's periodic controlled-substance inventory is expressly taken AS OF CLOSE of business on Friday, not at opening. Before closing, staff received a case of controlled medicine and moved it to the secured prescription area. A separate bottle remains quarantined for a quality investigation but is still in the pharmacy's physical custody. Purchasing records also list medication ordered from a supplier that has not been delivered and is not under the pharmacy's control. Which counting decisions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1304.11(a),(c),(e) (on hand and opening/closing inventory basis)

options.option_text: Count the afternoon receipt that was physically on hand before closing.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The close-of-business snapshot includes controlled substances under the registrant's control at that time.

options.option_text: Count stock that a supplier has invoiced but that remains outside the pharmacy's possession or control.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A mere undelivered purchase does not establish physical possession or control on the date of inventory.

options.option_text: Include the quarantined controlled bottle still held under the pharmacy's control.
options.original_rationale: Correct. On-hand inventory includes substances under registrant control, not only drugs available for dispensing.

options.option_text: Exclude the afternoon receipt because it arrived after the pharmacy opened.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. An inventory taken as of close includes receipts already on hand by closing time.

questions.question_stem: A corporate Massachusetts pharmacy has a current DEA registration and an employee with an otherwise valid power of attorney (POA) to execute paper DEA Form 222 orders. An administrative employee who signed the pharmacy's last DEA registration application, but is NOT a corporate officer, now wants to revoke that POA in November 2026. The corporate vice president is an authorized officer and two witnesses are available. What is required under the March 20, 2026 revision to 21 CFR 1305.05?

options.option_text: Only the employee holding the POA may terminate the arrangement, and the registrant cannot act without that consent.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 21 CFR 1305.05(b) permits a registrant to revoke the POA at any time.

options.option_text: Revocation requires destruction of every historical DEA Form 222 the employee previously signed, because records are void when POA authority ends.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Previously executed order records and powers of attorney have retention requirements; revocation is not deletion of history.

options.option_text: The administrative application signer can revoke the POA alone because signing the most recent registration application is sufficient federal authority.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. That older signatory language was specifically removed from §1305.05(c),(e) in 2026.

options.option_text: A corporate officer, not the last registration application signer, must execute revocation with two witnesses and written notice.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The current §1305.05(e) requires the registrant/partner/officer, as appropriate, and two witnesses; the notice and record duties remain.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy is registered as a DEA AUTHORIZED COLLECTOR with an approved collection receptacle. Three materials are presented on the same day: (X) a patient's lawfully held unused Schedule II tablets, (Y) expired Schedule II bottles that have never left the pharmacy's OWN inventory, and (Z) a partially used Schedule II dose generated by a hospital nursing unit. Which actions are appropriate as described? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: 21 CFR 1317.05(a), 1317.10, 1317.75(b)–(c); 21 CFR 1304.22 and applicable institutional accountability

options.option_text: The patient may deposit the ultimate-user medication into the pharmacy's authorized collection receptacle using the collection procedures.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 1317.75 permits qualifying ultimate users to deposit their own lawfully possessed controlled substances.

options.option_text: The pharmacy may pour its expired Schedule II stock into the ultimate-user take-back receptacle to avoid reverse-distributor documentation.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The authorized collection receptacle is not the lawful disposal route for the collector's own registrant inventory.

options.option_text: The pharmacy must account for or transfer its own expired controlled stock through an appropriate registrant-disposal/reverse-distributor process instead of treating it as patient take-back.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 21 CFR 1317.05(a), 1317.10 and applicable 1305 ordering/transfer rules govern registrant inventory disposal.

options.option_text: The nursing unit may drop partially administered hospital controlled-substance remnants into the pharmacy's public ultimate-user receptacle as though they belonged to a patient.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Institutional drug waste generated by a registrant is not simply an ultimate user's deposited medication; hospital controlled accountability/waste procedures apply.

questions.question_stem: A licensed Massachusetts hospital pharmacy receives two controlled-drug transactions from a nursing unit: Transaction X is an INTact, fully accountable Schedule II dosage unit that was never administered. Transaction Y is a partially used Schedule II injectable dose whose remaining portion is to be discarded after a documented patient administration. All identities and authorizations are valid. Which handling practices are appropriate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: MA DPH General Accountability Guidelines for Controlled Substances in Hospitals and Clinics with Pharmacies, Nursing Units, Schedules II–V; 105 CMR 700.005
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: DPH hospital/clinic accountability guidelines Nursing Units §Schedules II–V: perpetual inventory, unused partial disposal by two licensed staff co-sign
questions.scope_or_source_caveat: Official DPH online guide supports nursing-unit disposal and accountability; it does not individually enumerate each step for intact-unit return.

options.option_text: Document X's return from nursing-unit custody to pharmacy custody, reconciling the nursing-unit and pharmacy-controlled inventory records.
options.original_rationale: Correct. An unused accountable unit returned to stock custody is an inventory movement that requires traceability at both locations.
options.independent_option_analysis: Intact unused stock is inventory movement, not administration; reconcile on return.

options.option_text: Combine X's unused unit with Y's partially used residual and enter both as a single patient waste event.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. An intact unused return and a partially administered dose/waste have different origins; merging their records defeats inventory accountability.
options.independent_option_analysis: Combining untouched stock return and residual administered-dose disposal destroys separate accounting trails.

options.option_text: Document Y's administered amount and witnessed waste under institutional policy, with the applicable licensed witness and reconciliation of the unit-dose record.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Hospital controlled-drug accountability requires recording administered/wasted quantities and the witness, rather than treating residual drug as an intact pharmacy return.
options.independent_option_analysis: Remaining injectable portion is waste; DPH requires 2 licensed staff and co-sign unless policy stricter.

options.option_text: Record X as a partially administered patient dose to avoid entering any movement back to the pharmacy inventory.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Fabricating an administration record would obscure an unused return and compromise controlled-substance inventory accountability.
options.independent_option_analysis: Recording unused intact stock as administered is false inventory/administration documentation.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy arranges delivery of a refrigerated prescription to a customer's workplace. The patient has not designated a receptionist or alternate pickup location as an authorized agent. When a courier arrives, the patient has left and the receptionist offers to store the sealed carton in an unrefrigerated drawer until the next afternoon. The courier has not transferred custody, and the pharmacy has a written procedure for failed delivery and temperature excursions. What should the courier and pharmacy do?

options.option_text: Leave it with the receptionist.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. An unauthorized handoff does not ensure patient delivery or preserve prescribed temperature conditions.

options.option_text: Mark the package as delivered and ask the patient to collect it when convenient.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The proposed handoff has not been authorized and no actual patient/agent delivery occurred.

options.option_text: Keep custody and investigate safe redelivery.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Pharmacy delivery procedures must protect product integrity and prevent unauthorized handoff.

options.option_text: Store the package in a reception drawer and cancel the counseling offer.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Uncontrolled overnight storage does not satisfy stability or authorized-delivery requirements.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy sends a refrigerated prescription medication by courier to a patient's home. The insulated shipping container looks undamaged at delivery, but the temperature logger shows that the medication was exposed to a temperature outside its labeled storage range for an extended period. The manufacturer has not yet supplied stability data for that excursion. The patient requests that the courier leave the medication immediately. What is the BEST next step?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 9.02(2); 247 CMR 9.22(1),(4); Massachusetts Board pharmacy storage-shipping guidance

options.option_text: Release the product because a sealed undamaged outer carton proves the medication's chemical stability despite the logger result.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. A good-looking exterior is not evidence that the product remained within required storage conditions.

options.option_text: Hold the shipment, assess product integrity against stability evidence, and document the excursion before dispensing.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 9.02(2) requires shipping not to impair integrity and §9.22 requires an out-of-range response and medication-integrity assessment.

options.option_text: Ignore the logger because the medication was only in the courier's possession, not in the pharmacy's refrigerator.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The dispensing pharmacy remains responsible for packing, transportation and delivery processes that protect integrity.

options.option_text: Reset the package temperature indicator and leave the medication as long as the patient's name is correct on the label.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Replacing evidence or relabeling does not assess the quality of a temperature-exposed product.

questions.question_stem: Two Massachusetts-licensed retail pharmacies participate in two distinct SHARED PHARMACY SERVICE workflows. In Workflow A, Pharmacy 2 remotely checks a prescription and performs claims adjudication but never physically fills or labels it; Pharmacy 1 fills and dispenses it. In Workflow B, Pharmacy 2 also physically fills and sends the labeled medication back to Pharmacy 1 for patient handoff. Under Board Policy 2021-02 revised February 2025, which statements are accurate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

options.option_text: Workflow A is shared remote processing; Workflow B includes a central-fill activity because a second pharmacy physically prepares the patient's order.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The policy defines central fill by physical preparation at the second pharmacy and delivery to the original pharmacy.

options.option_text: Both arrangements automatically remove Pharmacy 1's liability for the prescription because Pharmacy 2 performed a portion of the work.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The policy makes participants jointly responsible for properly processed or filled prescriptions.

options.option_text: A remote-only processing arrangement can skip consent and audit trails because no physical medication is transferred to the second site.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The shared-service policy expressly covers remote processing and retains common safety and audit requirements.

options.option_text: Both workflows need the required secure common record, audit trail, patient notice/opt-out when retail, training and joint procedures.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Policy §III applies shared-service safeguards to all models; §IV has additional central-fill terms.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts originating retail pharmacy and a properly licensed central-fill pharmacy operate a compliant shared-service arrangement. The central-fill pharmacy robot prepared several Schedule VI patient-specific packages, which have now arrived at the originating pharmacy for patient pickup. Before any patient handoff, the manufacturer announces a LOT-specific recall covering one package. The originating pharmacy wants to distribute that package and let the central-fill partner handle the recall later because the robot made it. What should the pharmacy do?
questions.author_citation: MA Board Policy 2021-02 §§III(g)–(p), IV(a)–(b) (revised Feb. 6, 2025); 247 CMR 9.19(11) recall/quality duties

options.option_text: Release the affected package because a central-fill robot, not the dispensing pharmacy, is responsible for product quality at preparation.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Automation does not remove the originating or central-fill participants' joint shared-service responsibilities and patient safety duties.

options.option_text: Hold the recalled lot and coordinate with central fill through the shared audit trail; release only an appropriate unaffected product.
options.original_rationale: Correct. Under Board Policy 2021-02 each participant is jointly responsible for properly processed and filled orders, quality/safety, and traceable shared workflow; a known affected lot should not be released.

options.option_text: Send the recalled package to the patient unopened with a note that the patient may request a replacement later.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Knowingly distributing an affected recalled lot conflicts with product integrity, current recall duties and shared participant responsibility.

options.option_text: Change the label's lot number to an unaffected one so the package can still be sold without altering the robot's completed record.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Altering the package information does not change the physical drug lot or resolve the recall and compromises required audit records.

questions.question_stem: An inspection report cites two violations at a Massachusetts pharmacy, and the Board has given no alternative deadline. The manager proposes a general letter promising to 'improve compliance soon.' What does 247 CMR 9.25 require instead?
questions.exact_primary_provisions_reviewed: 247 CMR 9.25(1)-(5): correction plan within 21 days with violation-specific remedies

options.option_text: Submit a violation-specific correction plan within 21 days.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The regulation requires a specific written plan of correction for each violation within 21 days absent another Board deadline.
options.independent_option_analysis: Written plan due within 21 days absent Board alternative.

options.option_text: Only acknowledge receiving the report.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Mere acknowledgment does not satisfy the specified corrective-action plan requirement.
options.independent_option_analysis: Acknowledgment alone fails corrective plan requirements.

options.option_text: Only a commitment to retrain staff, without dates or assignment of responsibility.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The corrective plan must include an implementation date and responsible individual for each violation.
options.independent_option_analysis: Only retraining without dates/responsibility fails required elements.

options.option_text: No written response until an individual pharmacist faces disciplinary charges.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Facility inspection correction and individual licensure discipline are distinct processes.
options.independent_option_analysis: No requirement to await individual discipline before facility plan.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy stops dispensing for several days after flooding and uses its required COMPUTER-DOWNTIME plan while assessing damage. It then decides on November 1 to close PERMANENTLY on December 1. It has patient records and remaining controlled inventory, and served patients within the preceding 90 days. The manager proposes only to post a sign reading 'computer systems unavailable' and leave the records in the locked building after December 1. What is the best legal plan?

options.option_text: Follow the required planned-closure notices, record-transfer and controlled-inventory procedures instead of using only a downtime notice.
options.original_rationale: Correct. The 30-day planning interval permits the statutory 14-day advance closure duties, patient access and controlled-substance handling, plus postclosure filings.

options.option_text: Continue using the downtime plan without Board or patient closure notice, because the original cause was a flood.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Once permanent closure is planned, 247 CMR 6.13 closure procedures supersede reliance solely on a temporary outage process.

options.option_text: Simply email previous patients on the closing date and destroy their medication profiles to protect privacy.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Closure rules require advance patient notice and timely file transfers, not elimination of required records.

options.option_text: Leave untransferred controlled stock locked indefinitely; the pharmacist's active personal registration authorizes holding it after pharmacy closure.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Pharmacy closure entails compliant controlled stock transfer/disposal and return of licenses/registrations as required.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy will keep the SAME owner, manager of record, and staff but move its licensed dispensing operations to a NEW STREET ADDRESS. Management wants to treat the move as an ordinary online license renewal. The planned opening is 45 days away, and the Board has not granted an alternative application timetable or approved the new site. What is required before the pharmacy may operate at the new address?
questions.author_citation: 247 CMR 6.16 (relocation application, 90-day normal lead time and prior approval); 247 CMR 6.15 (distinct remodel)

options.option_text: The pharmacy may move immediately, provided the current license is posted at the new premises and the Board receives notice within 14 days.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. 247 CMR 6.16 requires advance Board approval before relocating; moving is not merely a posting or after-the-fact notification task.

options.option_text: The pharmacy may transfer the existing address registration without prior approval because the legal owner and manager have not changed.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Same ownership and MOR do not eliminate the separate licensed-premises relocation application/approval requirement.

options.option_text: Apply for Board relocation approval at least 90 days beforehand unless waived, and obtain approval before using the new address.
options.original_rationale: Correct. 247 CMR 6.16 explicitly requires a relocation application and payment, pharmacy layout drawings, and prior Board approval; the 90-day normal lead time may be varied by Board approval.

options.option_text: Obtain DEA approval only; the Massachusetts Board has no separate role in approving a pharmacy's move to a new address.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Controlled registration may be relevant but does not displace the Massachusetts relocation license rule.

questions.question_stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives a prescription for **Brand R**, a hypothetical extended-release Drug M tablet, 10 mg. The patient and prescriber allow lawful interchange. A supplied FDA-style therapeutic-equivalence table shows: Brand R = AB1; Generic P = AB1; Generic Q = AB2; Generic S = BX. Each generic has the same active ingredient, strength, dosage form and route; each is less expensive and reasonably available. Assume no other Massachusetts exception or clinical concern. Which generic is FDA-rated therapeutically equivalent to the prescribed product?
questions.author_citation: FDA Orange Book Preface §1.7 (AB/AB1/AB2), 105 CMR 720.050(a), 720.200 Appendix A; M.G.L. c.112 §12D

options.option_text: Generic P, because AB1 matches Brand R's exact therapeutic-equivalence group in the supplied FDA-style table.
options.original_rationale: Correct. FDA says products with three-character codes are therapeutically equivalent only to products with that same AB-number code.

options.option_text: Generic Q, because every AB-number code is therapeutically equivalent to every other AB-number code.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. AB1 and AB2 represent distinct equivalence groups in the FDA Orange Book; identical ingredients and strengths do not remove the distinction.

options.option_text: Generic S, because BX denotes an approved drug whose bioequivalence problems have all been resolved.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. BX is a B-category designation rather than an A-rated therapeutically equivalent comparison for the prescribed reference group.

options.option_text: Generic Q or Generic S, because either same-strength extended-release product qualifies without regard to its FDA code.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Same ingredient, route, dosage form and strength alone do not establish therapeutic equivalence when the FDA assigns different or B-category codes.

questions.question_stem: For a patient's prescription naming a particular reference biologic, the pharmacist checks the FDA's interchangeability classifications rather than relying on a wholesaler's marketing language. Product Y is an FDA biosimilar but has NO interchangeable designation for that reference product. Product Z is FDA-designated INTERCHANGEABLE with it. The prescriber has not given a written patient-specific prohibition against substitution, and the pharmacy has access to the patient's interoperable EHR. Which Massachusetts actions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.author_citation: M.G.L. c.112 §12EE(b)-(f); FDA Purple Book interchangeability classification

options.option_text: Product Y qualifies for automatic substitution solely because FDA has found it biosimilar.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. Massachusetts substitution requires the legally recognized interchangeable relationship, not biosimilarity alone.

options.option_text: Product Z may be selected under the interchangeable-biologic rule, subject to other requirements.
options.original_rationale: Correct. FDA interchangeability qualifies a product for the statutory substitution pathway when no patient-specific written ban applies.

options.option_text: No patient notification is needed if the prescriber receives a notice in the EHR.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The statute requires notifying the patient or authorized representative in writing as well as prescriber communication.

options.option_text: The substitution must be documented and communicated as required, including written patient notice.
options.original_rationale: Correct. M.G.L. c.112 §12EE requires prescriber notification, written patient notification and a retained substitution record.

questions.question_stem: During a shortage, Pharmacy A offers two transfers to Pharmacy B: one bottle to fill an already identified patient's prescription, and another bottle solely to replenish B's general stock. Which federal DSCSA distinction is correct?
questions.author_citation: FD&C Act §§581(19), 582(d)(1)(A)(ii); FDA DSCSA Product Tracing FAQ; other applicable CSA rules remain

options.option_text: Both are excluded because all transfers between retail pharmacies are emergency transactions.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The specific-patient-need exclusion does not extend to general stock replenishment.

options.option_text: Both transfers are exempt from tracing.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. The exclusion for fulfilling a specific patient need does not extend to replenishing general stock.

options.option_text: The general-stock transfer is excluded, but the identified-patient transfer is a wholesale transaction.
options.original_rationale: Incorrect. This reverses the statutory specific-patient-need exclusion.

options.option_text: Only the identified-patient transfer gets the DSCSA tracing exclusion.
options.original_rationale: Correct. FDA expressly distinguishes fulfillment for an identified patient from stocking in anticipation of future demand.
